headline: Connect under the trust anchors, the address and the identity check the request named, not the ones a second read answers with.
summary: `pki.transport.https` assembled its TLS trust list, read each per-request setting and framed the response through operations taken off the live prototype at the moment it used them, and read several of the caller's own settings twice: once to test whether they were set and again for the value it used. Where those two reads can disagree, the check and the connection decided differently. A private-address refusal the caller asked for was not applied, the name the handshake is verified against was replaced after it was checked, the caller's own identity hook disappeared after it had been found to be a function, and the trust list could be emptied so the platform's certificate store decided instead of the anchor the caller named. Every operation that module uses to reach a socket is now bound when the module loads, every setting is read once into the value both the test and the use see, and the addresses a resolver returns are snapshotted before they are classified. `guard.limits.cap`, which every decode bound in the toolkit passes through, is held to the same rule.

Fixed: `pki.transport.https` applies the private-address refusal the request asked for. `blockPrivateAddresses` was read once to test for presence and again for the value, so a value that answered `true` and then `false` left the refusal unarmed: measured, a request to `127.0.0.1` completed with the block in force. The same split applied to `tls.servername`, which is the name the server's certificate is verified against, to `tls.checkServerIdentity`, where the caller's hook was found to be a function and then not installed, to `tls` and `tls.anchors` themselves, to the transport's own `defaults.tls`, to `proxy`, and to `timeout` and `maxResponseBytes`. Each is now read once.

`pki.transport.https` connects under the trust anchors the request named. The list is assembled by appending to an empty array and the appending operation was read off the live prototype, so one answering with an empty array left the connection with no trust list of its own and the platform's certificate store decided instead: a caller that passed `tls.anchors` to pin one issuer was pinned to none of them. Measured against a loopback endpoint whose certificate only the named anchor trusts, the request then failed on the platform store's verdict rather than succeeding on the caller's. The proxy CONNECT path assembled its own trust list the same way.

The address a private-address check cleared is the address the connection is made to. A resolver that returns a list had its own entries forwarded to the socket layer, so an entry whose address answered a public value to the check and a loopback one afterwards reached loopback with `blockPrivateAddresses` set. Each address is now read once, that read is what is classified, and the snapshot is what is handed on.

A sparse proxy trust-anchor list is refused rather than read. The eligibility check walks the array's own property descriptors, which cannot see a gap, so a list whose gap was answered from the array prototype was validated as holding one anchor and converted as holding another: reading an array by index is specified to consult the prototype at a hole. A list with a gap is now refused as `transport/bad-proxy`.
The platform trust store is read through the provider bound when the module loads, so a replacement installed afterwards cannot answer with its own certificate list for a `useSystemStore` connection.

Every connection is opened through the function bound when the module loaded, not a property read off `node:https`, `node:http` or `node:tls` at the moment of the call: the request itself, the proxy CONNECT, the TLS connection made over a tunnel, and the one `pki.transport.peerChain` opens. A replacement installed afterwards sent a request prepared for one destination to another and handed the caller that peer's answer.

The socket itself is opened by this module rather than by the agent node builds, on the request and on the proxy CONNECT alike. `agent: false` does not mean no agent, which is what it had been relied on for: node builds one from the default agent's constructor, and that agent's own connection builder opened the socket, so replacing it returned a connection to another destination and the request went out over it. Measured, an `https:` request with `blockPrivateAddresses` set and certificate verification on reached a local plaintext listener that presented no certificate, and its body reached the caller. On the CONNECT path the same replacement could answer with a plain socket in place of the proxy's TLS connection, which is the request that carries `Proxy-Authorization`. The request options node computed for the hop are forwarded unchanged, so every TLS setting still applies, and there is still no connection pooling.

A per-request `tls.checkServerIdentity` keeps the transport's default from being read at all. The default was read whether or not the request overrode it, so a default supplied as an accessor ran even for a request that replaced it, and one that throws refused the request before it connected.

A response is as long as the bytes that arrived, and holds those bytes. It is allocated at the counted length and written through operations bound at load, because three earlier spellings were each steerable: a copy read off the prototype, a slice whose result is built through the species constructor, and a conversion that reads the received view's own `valueOf` and `length`. The last of those decided the length as well as the content: measured, an eight-byte response came back as 64 bytes with a `maxResponseBytes` of 8, so the size cap was reported as enforced on a body that exceeded it.

Every remaining operation `pki.transport.https` reaches a socket through is bound when the module loads: the PEM armor and IPv6 bracket scanners, the peer-chain walk, the anchor conversion, the TLS error classifier that decides whether a failure is reported as a trust failure or a transport one, the header names a proxy credential is stripped from, and the CONNECT tunnel's own options. The trust lists are assembled by copying and appending index by index, because appending with the built-in consults a spreading hook each argument can inherit, which replaced a validated anchor with another one.

`guard.limits.cap` compares a value against the bound it validated. `min` and `max` were each read more than once, with the integer check reading one value and the comparison another, so a bound answering a small integer to the check and a large one to the comparison configured a cap that admitted a value above its own limit. Each bound is now read once. No shipped verb could reach this, because every caller in the toolkit passes a fixed bound; the guard is what has to hold for the next one.
